blocks.prompt: The Tiny Rooms You Are Made Of
blocks.text: Cells are the tiny building blocks of every living thing. They are so small that a drop of water on your finger could hold millions of them. To see a cell, you need a microscope. Inside most cells is a round part called the nucleus. The nucleus is like the boss. It holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. Around the outside is a thin skin called the membrane. It decides what goes in and what comes out. You have trillions of cells. Right now, they are all working, and you cannot feel a thing.

blocks.prompt: The Man Who Named the Cell
blocks.text: In 1665, an Englishman named Robert Hooke built himself a microscope and started looking at everything he could find. One day he cut a very thin slice of cork, the same soft bark used to stopper a bottle, and slid it under his lens. What he saw surprised him. The cork was not solid at all. It was full of tiny empty boxes, packed together in neat rows like a honeycomb. Hooke needed a name for them. They reminded him of the small plain rooms where monks slept in a monastery. Those rooms were called cells. So he called the little boxes cells, and the name stuck. Here is the strange part. Hooke was not looking at living things. Cork comes from dead bark, so the boxes he drew were only the empty walls left behind. It took other scientists, with better lenses, to look into pond water and find cells that were alive and moving. But the name Hooke picked that day is still the one we use for the building block of every living thing on Earth.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Membrane: the guarded door
Nucleus: the vault holding DNA
Cytoplasm: the jelly everything floats in
Mitochondria: the power plants

blocks.prompt: A City the Size of a Speck
blocks.text: Open up a single animal cell and you find a place that runs like a small city, except the whole thing is far too small to see. Start at the edge. The cell membrane is a thin, flexible wall that holds everything in. It is not a sealed bag. It is more like a door with a guard: it lets food and oxygen in, pushes waste out, and keeps the rest of the world where it belongs. Inside, everything floats in a clear jelly called cytoplasm. Drifting in that jelly are the organelles, the working parts of the cell. Each one has a job. The nucleus sits near the middle, a round vault holding the cell's DNA. DNA is the instruction manual, and almost every cell in your body carries a complete copy of it. The mitochondria are the power plants. They take sugar and oxygen and turn them into energy the cell can spend. A busy muscle cell may hold thousands of mitochondria. A lazier cell holds far fewer. Here is what makes it interesting. Nearly all your cells carry the same instructions, and yet they do wildly different jobs. A red blood cell throws out its nucleus entirely to make room for oxygen. A nerve cell in your leg can stretch from your spine to your toes in one unbroken strand. A skin cell lives about three weeks and then flakes away. Same manual, different pages read.

notes: Cell theory has three parts

blocks.prompt: Every Cell Comes From Another Cell
blocks.text: For most of human history, nobody knew what living things were made of. You could cut open a leaf or a frog and see the parts, but the parts were made of something, and that something had no name. The answer arrived slowly, through glass. In 1665 Robert Hooke put a shaving of cork under a microscope and found it packed with empty boxes, which he named cells after the bare rooms monks slept in. A few years later, a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground lenses so fine that he could see further than anyone alive. He looked at pond water and found it swarming. He looked at scrapings from his own teeth and found creatures wriggling there too. He called them animalcules, little animals, and nobody quite believed him until the Royal Society checked for itself. It took nearly two centuries to assemble what those two men had glimpsed into a single idea. In 1838, Matthias Schleiden argued that every plant is built from cells. The following year, Theodor Schwann said the same of animals. That gave science two thirds of what is now called cell theory: all living things are made of cells, and the cell is the smallest unit that counts as alive. The third part is the strangest, and it took until the 1850s. Rudolf Virchow put it in Latin: omnis cellula e cellula. Every cell comes from a cell. Cells are not brewed out of ordinary matter. They are only ever made by splitting an existing one in half. Follow that rule backward and it does something dizzying. Every cell in you came from another cell, which came from another, in an unbroken chain running back through your mother, through her mother, through animals that were not human, through things that were not animals, all the way back to whatever cell first managed to copy itself billions of years ago. No link in that chain was ever skipped. Not once, in your entire ancestry, did the line go cold.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Mitochondria carry their own circular DNA
Endosymbiosis: the cell that moved in
Lynn Margulis argued it in 1967
Chloroplasts arrived the same way
Your mitochondrial DNA came from your mother
About 30 trillion human cells in you

blocks.prompt: The Bacteria That Moved In
blocks.text: Inside almost every cell in your body there are hundreds of small bean-shaped structures called mitochondria. They are the reason you can move, think, and stay warm. They take the sugar from your breakfast and the oxygen from your last breath and convert them into ATP, the molecule your cells spend the way you spend money. Stop your mitochondria and you stop, within seconds. For a long time they were treated as just another organelle, one more component in the machinery. Then people started noticing that mitochondria were behaving oddly for a component. They have their own DNA. Not a copy of yours: a separate, circular loop of genes, the same shape bacteria use. They have their own ribosomes for building proteins, and those ribosomes look more like a bacterium's than like the ones elsewhere in your cells. They cannot be built from scratch by the cell that houses them. They reproduce by pinching themselves in two, on their own schedule, exactly as bacteria divide. And they are wrapped in two membranes instead of one, as though something with a skin had once been swallowed by something else with a skin. In 1967 a young biologist named Lynn Margulis drew the obvious conclusion and was ridiculed for it. Her argument was that mitochondria are not parts. They are descendants. Roughly two billion years ago, she said, one ancient single-celled organism engulfed another and, for reasons nobody witnessed, failed to digest it. The swallowed cell kept living inside its host. It made energy. The host provided shelter and raw material. Neither could manage alone anymore, and over an enormous stretch of time the prisoner became an organ. Margulis called this endosymbiosis, living together on the inside. Her paper was rejected by about fifteen journals before one printed it. She was right. The genetic evidence that arrived in the following decades matched her claim so precisely that endosymbiosis is now taught as fact in the same textbooks that once refused to mention it. The chloroplasts that let plants eat sunlight came aboard the same way, in a separate takeover. Consider what that means about you. You are not one organism. You are a settlement. Every cell you own is a truce signed two billion years ago between two creatures that had no intention of cooperating, and the terms have held ever since. There is a final detail worth sitting with. Sperm contribute almost no mitochondria to an embryo, so the mitochondrial DNA you carry came from your mother, and from her mother before that, in a line of women running back further than any family name.
